ⓘ About this dashboard
Everything here is computed on your phone from the Vault — nothing is downloaded. Stocks that have not traded in the last 30 days of the Vault (delisted / merged) are left out. Market cap = Shares Outstanding × close (from the Shares/Float file); without that file, size groups fall back to rank by traded value. Large / Mid / Small are the top N / next N / the rest by market cap (editable below). Money trails are inferred from price and volume only (traded value = close × volume, and Chaikin money flow) — they are not FII/DII or delivery data.

Sectors vs the broad market, Alphatrace indices and the IPO index

🎯 Hunting Grounds
Find where the herd feeds — then hunt the strongest: Sector › Industry › Basic Industry › Stock
ⓘ How the hunt works
Pure momentum — no market cap. Every stock, industry and sector is scored 0–100 from its moving-average structure (price above the averages, averages sloping up, and ordered short over long). Stocks are scored against their own price, the equal-weight market, and their basic industry / industry / sector. The top slice of each basic industry is promoted to compete in its industry, then sector, then market (★ = levels survived). Groups are equal-weight indices built from the Vault; ⛶ opens a ratio chart on demand. Hunter ranks: Apex (everything aligned — the top predator), Charging (running hard), Ambush (strong trend, short-term dip — wait to pounce), Stalking (short-term waking up, long trend not yet), Wounded (weak), Carrion (downtrend — leave it). Chips along each row show dominance over each parent level (S, I, B = sector, industry, basic industry; T = the target).

Custom Indices — floating-market-cap-weighted synthetic index per Sector/Industry/Basic Industry, same methodology as Helios

⭐ My Indices — your own thematic / custom baskets (EV, defence, PSU banks…)

Markets — live 6-parameter snapshot direct from Vault, no historical backups. Pick the Chart view (Normal, Ratio, or Normal + Ratio together) and the Level (Sectors, Industries, Basic Industries, Stocks, or My Indices) from the two dropdowns, then press Compute this level. Ratio charts are a group divided by its parent (a stock ÷ its Basic Industry, a Basic Industry ÷ its Industry, an Industry ÷ its Sector); each level has its own ratio view, computed and remembered separately. In the combined view every row is followed by its ratio row (marked ↳ ratio); filters and sorting treat the pair together (a pair stays if either row passes the filter, and sorting uses the normal row). Tap a name to open its chart; a group name opens its synthetic index, a ratio row opens the ratio chart. Sector/Industry/Basic-Industry rows use the same synthetic-index engine as the Indices tab.

Zones — fresh pullback zones: one small-body candle (body ≤50% of its High–Low) per timeframe on Weekly and every multiple above it, linear (does not break the previous candle’s low for demand / high for supply), fresh (not revisited since the candle right after it) and below price (Demand) or above price (Supply). Tagged with the lower timeframe where the pullback shows a clean HH+HL / LH+LL structure, rated by the FVG it left (RDS). Timeframes that agree are merged into the highest. One row per stock; tap ⓘ for all its zones. Every column has a filter (numbers: >x, <x, a-b). Parameter filters below narrow by the 6-parameter family, measured on each zone's own timeframe, and add a strength score out of 6.

Update from feed — daily EOD bars from your GitHub feed (see eod-feed/README)

Methodology & downloads — daily EOD, classification and shares/float, from scratch

A · Daily EOD in the cloud (GitHub Actions — no phone needed)
  1. On GitHub create a public repo (NSE's bhavcopy is public data). Public is required so this app can read the files.
  2. Upload fetch_eod.py to the repo root and eod.yml as .github/workflows/eod.yml (GitHub: Add file → Create new file, type that path).
  3. Repo → Actions → “Daily EOD feed” → Run workflow. It creates eod/index.json and one CSV per trading day, then repeats at 7 pm and 9 pm IST on weekdays.
  4. In this tab, Update from feed: paste https://raw.githubusercontent.com/YOU/REPO/main/eod/ → Check → review → Apply. Tick “Check on open” (and “Auto-apply if clean”) for hands-free.
  5. If the run fails with HTTP 403, NSE is blocking GitHub's servers — use method B instead.
B · Daily EOD from your phone (Termux — works when A is blocked)
  1. Install Termux from F-Droid (not the Play Store build). Open it once.
  2. Download the .zip above. Android saves it to Downloads.
  3. In Termux, run these lines (short, so nothing gets truncated when pasted):
    termux-setup-storage
pkg install -y unzip
mkdir -p ~/kit && cd ~/kit
unzip -o ~/storage/downloads/alphatrace-eod-kit.zip
bash termux_setup.sh
  4. The script installs Python/git/cron, asks for your GitHub username, repo and a token (fine-grained, Contents: read & write on that one repo), pushes the kit, and schedules termux_daily.sh at 6:45 pm and 9:15 pm on weekdays.
  5. Test once: bash ~/alphatrace/termux_daily.sh — you should see “wrote eod/…csv” and “pushed”.
  6. Android may kill Termux: set Termux battery to Unrestricted and allow auto-start (ColorOS/OxygenOS).
  7. No NSE access at all that day? Download sec_bhavdata_full_DDMMYYYY.csv by hand and run python fetch_eod.py --file thatfile.csv.
C · Classification + shares/float (GitHub, monthly — input is your stocks.csv)
  1. In the same public repo upload stocks.csv (SYMBOL,SERIES), fundamentals.py, and fundamentals.yml as .github/workflows/fundamentals.yml.
  2. Optional but wise — probe one stock on your phone/PC: python fundamentals.py probe 500325. It prints BSE's raw reply; the builder maps Sector → MACRO_ECONOMIC_SECTOR, IndustryNew → SECTOR, IGroup → INDUSTRY, ISubgroup → BASIC_INDUSTRY (same layout as your nse_classification.csv). If a field is named differently, pass --sector-key etc.
  3. Repo → Actions → “Fundamentals” → Run workflow. About 30–60 minutes the first time; replies are cached, and it then re-runs by itself on the 1st of every month.
  4. It commits fundamentals/nse_classification.csv (SYMBOL, COMPANY_NAME, ISIN, SERIES, MACRO_ECONOMIC_SECTOR, SECTOR, INDUSTRY, BASIC_INDUSTRY, SOURCE), fundamentals/STOCKS_FLOAT.csv (Symbol, Short Name, Shares Outstanding, Float Shares), fundamentals/universe.csv (the clean stock list) and unmatched.csv.
  5. Shares and float come from Yahoo Finance (exact counts); anything Yahoo lacks falls back to BSE market cap ÷ price. unmatched.csv says why each symbol was left out — ETFs, funds and bonds are not companies, so they are never classified.
  6. Easiest: in the app use ⬇ Pull latest from GitHub (section F) — it fetches all of these for you. Manual route: ⭱ Import Classification → nse_classification.csv; ⭱ Import Shares/Float CSV → STOCKS_FLOAT.csv; then Import stock universe list → universe.csv and 🧹 Remove symbols not on the list. universe.csv is your clean stock list — stocks.csv itself still contains ETFs.
Not using the Pull button? Download the raw files from the repo page (⋯ → Download, or the file's “Raw” link). Nothing here needs your phone to stay on. In a real run roughly 2,440 stocks were classified and about 2,330 got shares/float; the rest are weighted equally until float data exists.
D · Daily prices (Yahoo, split-adjusted) — DAILY_OHLCV.csv
  1. Upload yahoo_ohlcv.py and ohlcv_daily.yml (as .github/workflows/ohlcv_daily.yml) to the repo that holds stocks.csv.
  2. Repo → Actions → “Daily OHLCV (Yahoo)” → Run workflow. It then runs every weekday at 9 pm IST.
  3. Output: ohlcv/DAILY_OHLCV.csv (latest trading day, every symbol; columns Date, Adj Close, Close, High, Low, Open, Volume, Symbol), plus ohlcv/daily/YYYY-MM-DD.csv for the last 90 days and ohlcv/missing.csv (symbols Yahoo has nothing for).
  4. Heads-up: this file covers everything in stocks.csv, ETFs included (≈ 2,900 symbols vs ≈ 2,440 stocks). ⬇ Pull latest from GitHub (section F) drops the ETFs using universe.csv. If you import by hand, import universe.csv first and run 🧹 Remove symbols not on the list afterwards.
  5. In the app: ⭱ Import OHLCV CSV → pick DAILY_OHLCV.csv (or several day files at once). Bars merge by date, so re-importing is harmless. A day with no Close yet is skipped, not guessed.
Yahoo's Close is already adjusted for splits and bonuses (the app uses it); Adj Close also removes dividends and is kept only for reference. NSE's own bhavcopy (methods A/B) is the official, unadjusted source — use either, or both.
E · Historical prices (one-time setup, 15+ years)
  1. Same repo: upload ohlcv_history.yml as .github/workflows/ohlcv_history.yml (it uses yahoo_ohlcv.py and stocks.csv).
  2. Actions → “Historical OHLCV (Yahoo)” → Run workflow; leave from_year at 2010 or change it. In a real run it took about 10–20 minutes.
  3. It commits ohlcv/history/HIST_OHLCV_<year>.csv.gz — one compressed file per calendar year (≈ 4 MB for 2010, growing to roughly 10 MB for recent years — older years have fewer listed stocks).
  4. Download those files, then in the app ⭱ Import OHLCV CSV / .gz and select all of them at once. The app unpacks .gz itself; it reports how many bars and symbols were merged.
  5. Order that works best: import the history first, then DAILY_OHLCV.csv.
  6. Splits and bonuses are applied by Yahoo retroactively. Re-run the workflow with from_year = this year − 2 every few months and re-import those files to keep recent history correct.
F · Pull from GitHub (one tap in the app — for classification, float, stock list and the latest daily prices)
  1. The repo must be public (it is, if you followed A). In Import → Pull from GitHub check the repo (owner/repo) and branch; they are remembered.
  2. Tick what you want: stock list, classification, shares/float, latest daily OHLCV, new listings (IPOs, section G). Tap ⬇ Pull latest from GitHub.
  3. Order used: fundamentals/universe.csv → fundamentals/nse_classification.csv → fundamentals/STOCKS_FLOAT.csv → ohlcv/DAILY_OHLCV.csv → ohlcv/new/NEW_OHLCV.csv (ETFs and any other symbols not on the list are left out of the price files).
  4. Each file goes through the same importer as picking it by hand, so each section reports its own counts. GitHub caches files for ~5 minutes — a pull right after a job finishes can return the previous version.
  5. The 15-year history is not pulled (too big for one tap) — import the .csv.gz files once with ⭱ Import OHLCV CSV / .gz (section E).
G · New listings (IPOs) — symbols that appear after your stocks.csv was made
  1. Upload new_listings.py and new_listings.yml (as .github/workflows/new_listings.yml) to the repo. Needs yahoo_ohlcv.py, fundamentals.py and stocks.csv already there.
  2. Actions → “New listings (IPOs)” → Run workflow. After that it runs by itself every weekday at 7:30 pm IST, before the 9 pm price job.
  3. Each run: (1) compares NSE's official list (EQUITY_L.csv, EQ and BE series only) with stocks.csv and appends every new symbol; (2) downloads the full price history since listing for everything listed in the last 120 days into ohlcv/new/NEW_OHLCV.csv; (3) refreshes classification and float (cached, so only the new ones are fetched); (4) adds the new symbols to fundamentals/universe.csv, because BSE often has no classification for a fresh IPO yet and the app would otherwise hide it.
  4. The log is ohlcv/new/new_listings.csv (SYMBOL, SERIES, LISTING_DATE, NAME, FIRST_SEEN). A symbol Yahoo has nothing on yet (usually the listing day itself) stays in the 120-day window and is retried every run.
  5. In the app: ⬇ Pull latest from GitHub with New listings (IPOs) ticked — it brings in the updated stock list, classification, float and the new symbols' history in one go.
First run: if your stocks.csv was missing older stocks too, they are added to the list, but only listings from the last 120 days get their history here — re-run the Historical OHLCV workflow (section E) to fill the rest. A brand-new IPO shows as unclassified until BSE publishes its sector data; the monthly Fundamentals run (or the next daily run of this one) picks it up. SME-board listings (SM/ST series) are ignored on purpose.

Data quality — flag or repair problems in yfinance-style OHLCV data

Scanning is read-only. Repairs come in two levels: safe (duplicate dates, zero/negative prices, high/low that don't contain open/close, empty placeholder bars) and judgement calls (one-bar price spikes that reverse, implausibly long wicks, apparent unadjusted splits — review before applying). Everything else is flag-only. Each fix backs the original bars up first. Synthetic IDX: indices are skipped — they're derived, not fetched.
Thresholds
Spike %: a one-day close move this large that mostly reverses the next day (default 22, just past NSE's widest standard 20% price band; a move on 3× or more normal volume is treated as a real event, not a bad tick). Wick %: a candle wick this far beyond the body (and 4× the local typical daily range). Gap days: calendar gap worth noting. Stale days: how far behind the vault's newest bar a symbol may end.

Backups

Continuity check — is every symbol's history unbroken?

Builds the market's own trading calendar from the vault (a day counts as a session when a good share of the stocks traded), then checks that every session between each symbol's first and last bar is present. It also lists weekdays with no data for any symbol (holidays — or a missing day) and symbols that stop early. Read-only; to repair, pull the affected range again.

Vault — browse, import, and export the raw OHLCV store directly (separate from the binary .atv1/.atvz importer in the top nav)

This is a first pass covering the core workflow — browse/search, import a plain OHLCV CSV, export per-symbol or the whole vault. Not a full port of every Helios Vault feature (backups/snapshots, Global Markets, listing-date inference, etc. aren't included here).
☁ Back up the vault to GitHub (.atvz)
Packs every real symbol into one compressed .atvz (the same file the importer reads) and stores it in its own folder of your private repo, split into 8 MB parts with a checksum. It uses the repo and token from Settings → ☁ Private backup (entered once). Built index and ratio charts are not included; they rebuild on demand. Restore merges by date, so nothing newer on this device is lost.

Benchmark for ratio charts — every Sector is ratio'd against this index; deeper levels drill from there

Alphatrace 500 — the top 500 stocks in the Vault by float market cap (float shares × latest close), used as the index every Sector is ratio'd against

Alphatrace 500 Momentum — float-cap weighted, momentum-tilted, with small & illiquid stocks screened out

ⓘ How this index is built
Every quarter-end (Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec) the index is rebuilt using only data available on that date. A stock must pass: float market cap, median daily traded value (last 60 sessions), few zero-volume days, and a minimum price. The 500 largest passing stocks by float cap form the universe.
Momentum score = average of 6-month and 12-month returns (skipping the latest month), each divided by the stock's volatility, then standardised. The top slice is held; each weight = float cap × a momentum multiplier (strong momentum up to ~4× , weak down to ~¼×), capped at the max weight. Between rebalances weights drift with prices; the index is chain-linked daily.
Limits: only stocks with Shares/Float data are considered, and delisted stocks missing from the Vault are not — so history carries some survivorship bias. Float uses today's share count.

Alphatrace IPO — every new listing since the date below, held for its first ~3 years, then graduates out

A stock counts as an IPO when its Vault history starts on or after the date below (new listings pulled from GitHub start on their listing day). It joins after the first sessions (so the listing-day pop is not counted), stays for the hold period, then leaves. Rebuild after pulling new listings.

Automated — compare any level of the classification tree with its own parent

Sector → the selected benchmark (Alphatrace 500 or Momentum, chosen above) · Industry → its Sector · Basic Industry → its Industry · Stock → its Basic Industry. Tap a row to drill in, tap "Open ratio" to compare it with its parent. The chart opens as a plain candlestick ratio — fully usable with every indicator, timeframe and tool the Chart tab already has. Next/Prev on the chart follows whatever's listed at the level you opened it from.

☁ Private backup & sync — to your own private GitHub repo, with full history

Tick what to back up, then ⬆ Push. On another device (or after a reset) use ⬇ Pull. Every push is a commit, so 🕘 History lets you restore an older version. Your GitHub token is never included in a backup.

      

      
ⓘ One-time setup

        
1. GitHub → New repository → name it e.g. alphatrace-backup → Private → tick “Add a README”.

        
2. Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens → Generate: repository access = only that repo, permission Contents: Read and write, expiry 90 days.

        
3. Paste the repo name and token above → ✔ Test (it tells you if the repo is private) → ⬆ Push now. Do the same on your other devices, then ⬇ Pull.

        
Pull replaces the local copy of whatever is ticked — a safety copy is kept for ↩ Undo. Don't edit the same thing on two devices without pulling first; the later push wins (older versions stay in 🕘 History).
